extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (PTAB litigators, patent prosecutors, post-grant counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate whether a patent qualifies for Covered Business Method (CBM) review and how §101 subject-matter-eligibility issues should be assessed at the PTAB, with attention to claim v. specification evidence and recent Federal Circuit guidance (Enfish, BASCOM, Rapid Litigation).

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM eligibility statutory two-prong
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent must: (1) claim a method or apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service; and (2) not claim a technological invention. (AIA § 18; 37 C.F.R. § 42.301(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBM review differs from IPR/PGR in that non-prior-art challenges (e.g., § 101 and § 112) are available in CBM and estoppel is narrower. Both prongs must be satisfied for CBM institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial product or service prong — focus on claims
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB increasingly requires that the financial aspect be shown in the claims rather than relying on the specification alone; claim language must demonstrate a link to financial activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent denials (e.g., CoreLogic, AT&T Mobility) found that specification examples of billing or revenue models were insufficient absent claim language. Conversely, dependent claim recitations tied to revenue (e.g., 'advertising data') have supported eligibility (iBiquity). When drafting or petitioning, emphasize claim elements that manifest financial activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification vs. claim evidence — when the specification can suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the PTAB has trended toward requiring claim language, there are cases where the specification's teaching that an element is used to generate revenue can establish CBM-eligibility (e.g., iBiquity relied on specification teaching that 'advertising data is used to generate revenue').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because panels are inconsistent, cite both claims and specification where possible; dependent claims that tie generic elements to financial uses strengthen CBM eligibility arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could be used for a financial service vs specifically intended for such use
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB distinguishes inventions that merely could be used for financial products/services from inventions specifically intended for financial use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions (e.g., ServiceNow, Par Pharmaceutical) show that mere potential for financial use (e.g., ATM example) is insufficient absent claim-specific limitation or specification support establishing financial purpose or monetary consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: No one-size-fits-all; panel inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB panels have reached divergent outcomes on similar facts; some panels infer financial status from specification where unequivocal, others require claims to show financial nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare for inconsistent panel treatment (see Motorola Mobility split panel outcomes); build multiple lines of support (claim language, dependent claims, specification, prosecution history) when arguing CBM eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM practical recommendation — heightened scrutiny requires careful consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the PTAB has increased reliance on the financial prong as a basis to deny CBM petitions, the financial aspect must be given careful consideration when evaluating a patent’s eligibility for CBM review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing petitions or preparing patents, evaluate whether claim language, dependent claims, or specification examples unmistakably connect the invention to a financial product/service; absent that, institution risk is elevated.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 Alice framework — look at the claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the two-step Alice test: (1) whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, natural phenomenon), and (2) if so, whether the claim as a whole is significantly more than that exception. The Federal Circuit emphasizes examining the claim as a whole and its purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid Litigation, Enfish, and BASCOM emphasize that simply identifying a judicial exception is insufficient; consider whether the claim uses a phenomenon to attain a distinct end or transforms it into an inventive application. Arguments should treat the claim holistically, including purpose and ordered combination of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enfish guidance for computer-related claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-related patents, ask whether claims are directed to an improvement to computer functionality rather than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enfish supports finding eligibility where claims improve computer functionality (example: self-referential table). The PTAB has cited Enfish but its impact has been limited and fact-dependent; compare claim features to Enfish's improvement characteristics when making or opposing §101 arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: BASCOM guidance — ordered combination can confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual elements are conventional, an inventive ordered combination of elements may render the claim 'significantly more' than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BASCOM remanded where the lower tribunal failed to explain why the ordered combination was conventional. In briefing, address whether the combination of conventional components yields a non-conventional whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and completeness of petitioner’s §101 analysis at PTAB
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner must analyze claims as a whole and provide sufficient proof; incomplete analyses or failure of proof can lead to denial of institution under §101 (e.g., Walgreen denial where petitioner’s analysis was incomplete).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure petitioners fully address each claim element, the 'select code' or other specifics, and do not rely on selective snippets of the specification. Anticipate PTAB scrutiny on completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR availability and scope for §101 challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Grant Review (PGR) can include §101 ineligibility grounds, but only patents filed after March 16, 2013 are subject to PGR; PGR has not commonly been used for §101 so far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most §101 challenges at the PTAB occur in CBM reviews (which can reach older patents) rather than IPRs (which cannot). Assess whether the patent's filing date and subject matter make PGR or CBM the appropriate vehicle for a §101 challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical impact of Federal Circuit scrutiny on PTAB practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent Federal Circuit reversals (Enfish, BASCOM, Rapid Litigation) have increased scrutiny on how §101 is applied, influencing PTAB caution in explaining ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may benefit patent owners in close cases (PTAB may exercise greater care) and could result in more borderline patents surviving. Consider how Federal Circuit precedent might be leveraged in PTAB briefing and how the PTAB may change its decision-writing to withstand review.
